turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come through, bed's free if he'll hop up. What's brought you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's his skin, doctor. Dry patches behind both knees and in the elbow creases, and he's scratching them raw, especially at night.
[SEG0003] person_3 (PATIENT): Itchy.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right. Itchy dry patches behind the knees and in the elbows, worse at night. How long's that been going?
[SEG0005] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Umm, I was gonna say three weeks. No, hang on, his birthday was six weeks back, so it's six weeks.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Six weeks. Does it hurt as well, mate, or just itch?
[SEG0007] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Itchy.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ok. Any fever with it? And is he eating normally?
[SEG0009] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No fever. Eating's fine. He's just not sleeping, up scratching for half the night.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Is the skin weeping at all, or any pus?
[SEG0011] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No weeping and no pus. Just dry and flaky. It bleeds a tiny bit sometimes where he scratches.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): What are you putting on it?
[SEG0013] person_3 (PATIENT): Umm. The white cream for the itchy bits. The yellow one at night for the dry skin. And only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me say that back. White cream for the itch, yellow cream at night for the dryness, Ayurvedic powder in the morning. Mum, what are the actual doses?

[SEG0015] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The white one is the hydrocortizone. I nearly said nought point five percent, no, it's the one percent, a pea-sized amount twice a day. The yellow tube is QV, just a thick layer at night. He's had eczema since he was a bub, that's what we use the white one for.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the powder, do you know which one?
[SEG0017] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I don't know the proper name. It's just an Ayurvedic powder from the grocer. He has a pinch by mouth in his milk every morning. I doubt it does much.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mm. We'll park that as an unnamed powder. Anyone in the family with asthma?
[SEG0019] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His dad has asthma, yeah. Been on a puffer for years.
[SEG0020] person_3 (PATIENT): Daddy's puffer is purple.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's your dad's, not yours. Any cough or wheeze in this little one?
[SEG0022] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No cough, no wheeze. He runs around fine.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): How about his tummy or his waterworks, anything there?
[SEG0024] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No. All fine.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll have a look. Behind both knees and both elbow creases the skin's dry and thickened, scratch marks, no pus. Couple of small soft glands in the neck.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest is clear, breathing's easy, and his tummy's soft.
[SEG0027] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sorry he wriggles. Err, we were late, the carpark was a shocker.

[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): All good. So, six weeks of itchy dry patches in the creases, worse at night, scratching, not infected. Hydrocortisone one percent twice a day, QV at night, and a pinch of that powder each morning. I think this is an eczema flare.

[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll change the steroid. Stop the hydrocortisone, start Advantan fatty ointment nought point one percent, a thin layer once a day on the patches only, for seven days, then stop it.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep the QV, but three times a day, not just at night, and again within a few minutes of a short lukewarm bath. Skip ordinary soap on those patches.
[SEG0031] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Three times a day, and after his bath. He already has a bath most nights. I can do that.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll book the nurse to take bloods Thursday morning, a full blood count and an IgE. No fasting, breakfast is fine, just have him here around 8.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): If those are borderline we do the third test, a RAST panel. Not ordering that today. And if the neck glands do not settle, we'll organise an ultrasound.
[SEG0034] person_3 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Will the needle hurt?
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Quick pinch, then it's done. I'll see you back in two weeks for a skin check and those results.
[SEG0036] person_2 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Thursday for the bloods, back in two weeks. We'll grab the Advantan from the chemist. Thanks.

spec.situation: Mother brings a child with itchy dry patches behind the knees and elbows, worse at night, scratching; creams named by colour; father has asthma; doctor adjusts steroid cream and moisturiser advice.

traps.happens: The patient lists medicines with their purpose ('amlodipine for the pressure', 'the cholesterol one at night', 'sugar tablets') and also mentions a herbal or shop remedy in passing ('only the Ayurvedic powder in the morning'). Their chronic conditions are never asked about directly.
traps.label_rule: Each medicine is recorded with the dose and timing said for THAT medicine; the herbal remedy is a medicine too (currently_used). A condition the patient states through its medicine ('for the pressure') is a past_medical_history entry ONLY if the patient actually said the condition name or its everyday name ('the pressure' = hypertension, normalized); do not invent a duration.

traps.happens: In the plan the doctor books some tests or visits for a definite time ('the nurse takes bloods Thursday morning', 'I'll see you in two weeks') and makes others conditional ('if those are borderline we do the third test', 'if it does not settle, a scan').
traps.label_rule: Booked or arranged = status planned. Only the hedged ones are conditional. Never mark a booked test conditional or 'if needed'. Instructions for the booked test (fasting, time, medicine timing) belong to that test's action, not a separate invented plan item.

features: self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.

bad.reason: Advantan 0.1% once daily for seven days is stated, but generic name is not mentioned.
bad.text: Advantan fatty ointment (generic_name=methylprednisolone aceponate, dose=0.1%, frequency=once a day, duration=7 days, indication=eczema flare, status=planned, reported_by=doctor)

omissions.text: Advantan fatty ointment should be applied as a thin layer to the patches only; this application instruction is missing from the planned medication entry.
QV use was changed from nightly to three times a day; the recorded current medication still lists QV as 'at night' without capturing that this regimen was superseded by the doctor's plan.
The doctor advised applying QV again within a few minutes of a short lukewarm bath.
The doctor advised to skip ordinary soap on the affected patches.
Follow-up was specifically for a skin check and review of blood results, not just a generic consultation.
The planned blood tests were specified as full blood count and IgE around 8 am Thursday morning.
Negative finding: the child runs around fine / good exercise tolerance.
